findings.title: Private-IP check is a separate DNS lookup from the connection (rebinding / TOCTOU)
findings.evidence: _reject_non_public_host resolves the host with socket.getaddrinfo and rejects non-global answers, but the fetch on line 57 is a plain requests.get(current, ...) that resolves the same name again inside urllib3; the address that is validated is never the address that is connected to. Anything that changes the answer between the two lookups (attacker-influenced DNS for an allowlisted name, short-TTL round robin, split-horizon resolver) yields a connection to an address the guard never saw, which is exactly the SSRF case the module claims to stop in its docstring.
findings.recommendation: Resolve once, validate the resulting address, and connect to that pinned address (e.g. a requests adapter or transport that accepts a pre-resolved IP and sets Host/SNI), or drop the pretence that the resolver check protects the connection and rely solely on the host allowlist plus egress policy. Also note requests honours HTTP(S)_PROXY from the environment by default, which routes the request through a third party that does its own resolution; if the DNS check is meant to matter, use an explicit

findings.title: Response is left open when raise_for_status raises, and callers are never told to close it
findings.evidence: On the non-redirect path the code calls response.raise_for_status() and only then returns the response; if the status is 4xx/5xx the exception propagates and the connection is never released, so repeated failed fetches leak sockets until the pool/GC catches up. The success path also hands back an open response with no close contract in the docstring.
findings.recommendation: Wrap the status check in try/finally with response.close() on the error path, or document that the caller owns and must close the returned response; preferably always read/close inside safe_fetch and return status plus body.

findings.title: No response size limit: allowlisted host can return an unbounded body into memory
findings.evidence: The request is issued without stream=True and without reading the body in chunks, so requests buffers the entire payload. A compromised or misbehaving allowlisted host (or a redirect chain ending at one) can exhaust memory; the 10 second timeout bounds time, not bytes.
findings.recommendation: Use stream=True with a maximum byte count (iter_content chunks, abort past the limit), or enforce a Content-Length ceiling before reading the body.

findings.title: 3xx statuses outside REDIRECT_STATUSES are returned as if the fetch succeeded
findings.evidence: The redirect set omits 300 and 304, and requests.raise_for_status() only raises for 4xx/5xx, so a 300 Multiple Choices (or a 304 from a caching intermediary) on line 60 falls into the non-redirect branch and is returned to the caller as a successful fetch with no error and no body.
findings.recommendation: Treat any 3xx as either a redirect (if Location is present) or an explicit error, e.g. reject response.is_redirect or check 300 <= status < 400 explicitly before falling through to raise_for_status.

findings.title: No tests accompany the redirect revalidation and non-public-address rejection
findings.evidence: The diff adds only the module; the risky branches (per-hop revalidation on line 56, non-global resolution rejection, the MAX_REDIRECTS cutoff, and a redirect to a non-allowlisted host) have no coverage, and the change reports that no test commands were run, so regressions in the security-relevant control would go unnoticed.
findings.recommendation: Add tests with a stubbed resolver and a mocked transport covering: redirect to 127.0.0.1 / 169.254.169.254 / non-allowlisted host rejected, exactly MAX_REDIRECTS redirects succeeding and MAX_REDIRECTS+1 raising, redirect without Location raising, and a non-443 or credentialed URL rejected.
